source.title: Diametrical Risk Minimization: theory and computations

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper; no garbling or truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own neural-network training experiments and evaluates test accuracy and local empirical-risk neighborhoods, using a different training intervention (diametrical risk minimization) from the claim versions. Its experiments use label-corrupted data and do not directly test any listed version.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on fitting noisy labels and generalizing on natural labels, but those cited findings are not rows. Its own results compare SGD-DRM and SGD-ERM on label-corrupted data; the reported accuracy curves are figures, with qualitative outcomes also described in the text.
record.test_reason: The study uses prior findings about noisy-label memorization and flat minima to motivate DRM, then evaluates DRM against ERM. Its own experiments do not test any listed version: 50% corrupted labels do not establish V1's natural-label versus random-label comparison, and fixed-radius perturbations do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or rank generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors report reduced overfitting and flatter empirical-risk neighborhoods for DRM on the tested corrupted-label tasks. They also establish bounds on true risk relative to diametrical empirical risk, independent of Lipschitz moduli under stated assumptions, and acknowledge computational costs and unresolved hyperparameter choices.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments compare standard SGD for ERM with SGD-DRM, which minimizes an approximation to worst-case empirical risk over parameter perturbations. The main experiments use 50% incorrectly flipped training labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The results differ between fully connected networks and ResNet20: for ResNet20, the authors report nearly zero test-accuracy degradation for SGD-DRM, while the fully connected CIFAR-10 model shows a trend similar to MNIST. DRM radius also differs by dataset and architecture: γ = 10 for MNIST, γ = 5 for fully connected CIFAR-10, and γ = 1 for ResNet20.

fits_no_version.finding: On three-class MNIST and CIFAR-10 with 50% incorrect training labels, DRM maintains better test accuracy than ERM; the extended MNIST run still shows some DRM degradation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Diametrical risk minimization can reduce overfitting relative to empirical risk minimization on partially label-corrupted classification tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed layer-wise perturbations produce smaller increases in empirical loss around DRM solutions than ERM solutions. The solutions have different empirical losses, and perturbations are not scaled to weight magnitudes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DRM can find solutions with flatter fixed-radius empirical-loss neighborhoods than ERM in the tested corrupted-label tasks.

record.problems: The reported accuracy curves are figures without numeric values in the text; no uncertainty estimates are given. Experiments use three-class subsets of MNIST and CIFAR-10 with 50% label noise. DRM training takes approximately 3-5 times longer than ERM training with the same architecture and data, according to the paper.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Neighborhood empirical-risk distributions in Figures 2c–2d and 3c–3d measure local loss flatness rather than the test-error gap named by a version; they are not included as version-bearing rows.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fixed random-label training, near-perfect random-label fit, and chance held-out accuracy under random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
A comparison establishing an architectural generalization advantage and the contribution of local connectivity. The two architectures are used to evaluate DRM.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance among similarly fitted networks, its association with training–test gaps, and its ranking against norm and margin measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The neighborhood results are already declared in rows_left_out, so they require no missing entry. All row states concern applicability to the listed versions; cannot_determine does not mean the qualitative DRM-versus-ERM outcomes are unreadable.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report its own experiment comparing natural-label and random-label training outcomes.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks as an architecture-bias test.
The paper compares local empirical-risk neighborhoods for DRM and ERM solutions, but does not test magnitude-aware sharpness as a measure that ranks generalization gaps.
No removal of memorized training examples.
